acceptedAnswer.text: Your bracket is the rate on your last dollar of taxable income, which is your income after the deduction. A single filer with $85,000 of income has $68,900 of taxable income and lands in the 22% bracket. Enter your own income and filing status in the calculator above to see yours.

mainEntity.name: What tax bracket am I in?

acceptedAnswer.text: Subtract your deduction from your income, then find the band that holds your last taxable dollar. For a single filer, the 22% band covers taxable income over $50,400 up to $105,700. The calculator above does both steps and names the bracket for you.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate your tax bracket?

acceptedAnswer.text: The marginal rate is the rate on your last taxable dollar, and the effective rate is your total tax divided by income before deductions. A single filer with $85,000 of income has a 22% marginal rate. The same filer's effective rate is 11.6%, because $9,870 of tax is spread across all $85,000.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a marginal and an effective tax rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Only the dollars inside the higher band are taxed at the higher rate. A single filer whose taxable income rises past $105,700 pays 24% on the dollars above that line. The tax on every dollar below $105,700 stays the same.

mainEntity.name: Does moving into a higher bracket mean all my income is taxed more?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2026 federal rates run from 10% to 37% across seven brackets. For a single filer, the top 37% rate starts above $640,600 of taxable income. The 2026 tax brackets guide lists every threshold for each filing status, and the projected 2027 brackets cover the following year. The figures come from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Revenue Procedure for the 2026 tax year.

mainEntity.name: What are the 2026 federal tax brackets?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2026 standard deduction is $16,100 for a single filer. It is also $16,100 for married filing separately, $32,200 for married filing jointly and $24,150 for head of household. The calculator uses it by default unless you enter a custom deduction. The amounts appear in the IRS release on the 2026 adjustments.

mainEntity.name: What is the standard deduction for 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: In this calculator, a deduction larger than the standard deduction is what lowers taxable income. A single filer with $68,900 of taxable income must get it to $50,400 or less to reach the 12% bracket. That takes $18,500 more in deductions, so enter a custom total above to test it. This page does not give personal tax advice.

mainEntity.name: How do I lower my taxable income to drop a bracket?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The calculator covers federal ordinary-income brackets only, with no state tax. It also leaves out payroll tax, credits, capital gains rates and the qualified business income deduction. Add your state tax separately, and browse all calculators for other money tools. To estimate your take-home pay after payroll tax, use the paycheck calculator.

The tax bracket calculator above finds your taxable income by subtracting a deduction from your income before deductions. It uses the standard deduction unless you enter your own total. Add your filing status to see your 2026 federal bracket, estimated tax and effective rate, plus the room left before the next bracket starts. For example, take a single filer with $85,000 of income and the $16,100 standard deduction. Taxable income is $68,900, so the top dollars land in the 22% bracket and the tax comes to $9,870. That is an effective rate of 11.6%, with $36,800 of room before the 24% bracket starts. The 2026 standard deduction is $16,100 for a single filer and for married filing separately. It is $32,200 for married filing jointly and $24,150 for head of household, and your filing status also sets where each bracket starts. Tax is figured band by band, so only the dollars inside each band are taxed at that band's rate. For the single filer in the example above, the first $12,400 of taxable income is taxed at 10%, which is $1,240. The next $38,000 is taxed at 12%, which adds $4,560. The last $18,500 is taxed at 22% for $4,070, and that top band sets the marginal rate, which is the rate of the highest band holding any taxable dollar. The effective rate divides total tax by income before deductions, so $9,870 on $85,000 comes to 11.6%. Room left is the taxable income you can add before the next bracket starts, which is $36,800 here because the 24% band begins at $105,700. A married couple filing jointly with $150,000 of income lands in the 22% bracket at an effective rate of 10.2%. A head of household with $60,000 of income owes $3,948 and sits in the 12% bracket. A single filer with $250,000 of income reaches the 32% bracket, but the effective rate is 20.5%. The calculator applies ordinary-income brackets only, so it leaves out credits, capital gains rates, the qualified business income deduction, payroll tax and state tax. It is the wrong tool if you need a full return, owe self-employment tax or have capital gains, and ordinary income vs capital gains tax covers capital gains rates.
